title: "Asymmetric Speed–Accuracy Dependence Beyond PISA"

  The standard hierarchical model for speed and accuracy assumes a person's

  Thirty splits of one assessment cannot tell you whether that is a fact about

## Motivation

The hierarchical framework of @vanderlinden2007hierarchical is the standard
way to model response accuracy and response time together. Level 1 is
familiar: a 2PL for whether each answer is right, a lognormal for how long it
took. Level 2 is the part that does the joining — it says a person's latent
ability $\theta$ and latent speed $\tau$ are drawn together from a **bivariate
normal**.

That second level is an assumption, and a strong one. A bivariate normal is
*radially symmetric*: whatever dependence exists between ability and speed, it
has to be the same shape in opposite corners of the joint distribution. If
unusually fast-and-wrong respondents cluster much more tightly than unusually
slow-and-right ones, a bivariate normal cannot say so. It has one correlation
and no way to put more structure in one tail than the other.

@kwon2026copula replace that bivariate normal with a **copula**, which
separates the dependence structure from the marginals and so can be asymmetric
and tail-concentrated. Fitting their model to 30 splits of PISA 2018, they find
a 90°-rotated Joe copula selected over the normal on 28 of them, and read this
as "strong evidence for the presence of asymmetric tail dependence in
large-scale educational assessments."

Thirty splits of one assessment is a narrow base for a claim about item
response data in general, and the paper's own non-PISA evidence does not widen
it much. Alongside PISA it fits the same nine models to six smaller datasets —
five cognitive-training tasks and a novel object memory test — and there the
bivariate normal is selected on four, a 270°-rotated Gumbel on two, and the
90°-rotated Joe on none. Within PISA itself the picture is also uneven: across
the thirty country-by-cluster cells they fit individually, the 90°-rotated Joe
is selected on fourteen of the fifteen science cells but only five of the
fifteen in mathematics, where the bivariate normal takes eight. Their headline
direction is, on their own showing, strongest in one subject of one
assessment. That makes the generalisation question a real one rather than
a rhetorical one: **does the direction and magnitude of that tail asymmetry
show up outside large-scale educational assessment, or is it a PISA fact?**
The IRW holds much more heterogeneous material to ask it of — and one of the
paper's own six is an IRW table that this pass also analyses, so part of the
answer is a re-examination of their evidence rather than a new sample.

### What biases this screen, stated up front

This page is **not** the paper's estimator. It is a deliberately simple
two-stage screen: fit the plain bivariate-normal hierarchical model, take the
resulting person estimates $(\hat\theta, \hat\tau)$, and characterise *their*
empirical copula.

The direction of the resulting bias is knowable in advance and belongs here
rather than in the Limitations. $\hat\theta$ and $\hat\tau$ are shrunken
posterior means from a model whose person prior **is** the bivariate normal.
Shrinkage pulls the joint distribution toward its centre, and pulling toward
the centre is exactly what destroys tail dependence. So this screen is
**conservative**: it is biased toward finding *no* asymmetry.

That asymmetry of evidence is what makes the screen worth running at all.
Asymmetry it *does* find should therefore be credible, because it had to
survive a procedure that works against it, while absence of asymmetry on any
given table is weak evidence of absence.

That is the argument, and one result below strains it: on the single dataset
this page shares with the paper, the two methods disagree in the direction the
argument says they should not. Because that is a threat to the whole design
rather than to one row, it is tested directly — by generating data from an
exactly bivariate normal prior and asking how often the screen reports
asymmetry anyway. It does not. The result and its limits are set out below.

### Related pages

[Response time and accuracy: an IMV analysis](rt_imv.qmd) asks the
*response-level* version of this question — whether within-item-centred
$\log(\mathrm{RT})$ improves prediction of individual responses over a Rasch
baseline, keyed to @domingue2022notsofast. That is a different object: this
page is about the *person-level* joint distribution, not about predicting
individual responses. [Guessing](guessing.qmd) matters here too, for a reason
that only becomes clear once the winning family is identified below.
[Asymmetric item response functions](asymmetric_irt.qmd) and
[bits per item](bits_per_item.qmd) ask the analogous question about the
item side: whether a more flexible shape buys anything.

## Data and methods

### Dataset selection

The starting pool is every IRW table that carries an `rt` column, is
dichotomous, and is big enough for a claim about tails to mean anything.

```{r}
#| label: filter-datasets
#| eval: false

# From irw_metadata() rather than irw_filter() alone: the gates that matter
# here are density and responses-per-unit facts that irw_filter() does not
# express.
pool <- meta[has_rt &
             meta$n_categories  == 2 &
             meta$n_participants >= 300 &
             meta$n_items        >= 10, ]
```

`r r_all_candidates` tables met that criterion as of
`r format(date_run, "%B %Y")`. That number is a *starting* pool, not a run
list, and the gap between the two is itself a corpus fact worth reporting.

### Two gates, and why a density number is not enough

**Repeated trials are not an item response matrix.** A hierarchical
speed–accuracy model wants one response and one response time per
person–item. When a table's density runs far above 1, the `id`–`item` key
repeats — but for two quite different reasons, and density alone cannot tell
them apart. Checking the actual keys separates them cleanly:

- For `rapm_poulton_2022_timed` / `_untimed` (two waves) and
  `quopl2_forster_2021_quop` (eight waves), the `wave` column resolves the
  duplicates **exactly** — zero repeated `id`–`item` pairs within a wave.
  Keeping the first wave is then a real collapsing rule, and those tables stay.
- For the five `enkavi_2019_*` tables, duplicates survive both `wave` *and*
  `position`. There, `item` names a **stimulus type presented many times**, not
  a distinct item. No person-by-item matrix exists to put the model on, so
  those tables are excluded rather than reshaped. The same holds for
  `imps2025_hf`, which is four items over sixty-nine trials.

**Sparsity has two different victims.** Reporting a table as simply "sparse"
hides which part of the model it breaks. The floors are therefore set per unit:
at least **`r min_rpi` responses per item** and at least **`r person_floor` per
person**. The Duolingo tables show why the distinction matters — they carry
150–450 responses per *person*, which is ample, but as few as 3.6 per *item*.
There the item parameters are the noise source, and because $\hat\theta$ is
computed from item parameters, poisoning them poisons the person estimates too.

Tables wider than `r max_items` items are fitted on their
`r max_items` most-administered items and flagged as item-selected subtables;
they are reported separately below and never pooled with the rest. Tables with
more than `r format(max_n, big.mark = ",")` respondents are downsampled, which
is a compute decision and not a statistical one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-attrition
#| tbl-cap: "Why candidate tables did not produce a result. Exclusions are recorded with their reason rather than silently dropped."

if (nrow(excluded_df) > 0) {
  excluded_df |>
    count(reason, name = "n_tables") |>
    arrange(desc(n_tables)) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Reason excluded", "N tables"))
} else {
  knitr::kable(tibble(Note = "No candidate table was excluded in this pass."))
}
```

Of the `r r_n_tables_run` candidate tables in this pass,
**`r nrow(summary_df)`** produced usable results.

### Per-table computation

For each surviving table, `fit_one_table()`:

1. Fetches the table and resolves repeated `id`–`item` keys as described above,
   coercing `rt` explicitly — it does not always arrive numeric — and dropping
   non-positive times, which $\log$ would send to $-\infty$.
2. Applies the item and person response floors, iterated twice, since dropping
   thin items can push a person below the person floor and vice versa.
3. Fits the **bivariate-normal hierarchical model** with `LNIRT`
   [@fox2021lnirt], `r format(xg, big.mark = ",")` MCMC iterations, and takes
   the posterior means $\hat\theta$ (ability) and $\hat\tau$ (speed, where
   higher means faster).
4. Converts the pair to pseudo-observations (ranks) and selects a copula
   family by AIC, recording the full AIC table rather than only the winner.
   The candidate set here extends the paper's rather than matching it.
   @kwon2026copula compare the bivariate normal against Gumbel and Joe in all
   four rotations — nine models — and select by log-likelihood, which is
   reasonable there because all nine carry one dependence parameter. This page
   adds **independence** and the **Student $t$** as reference points, and so
   selects by AIC instead, the $t$ carrying one parameter more than the rest.
5. Computes tail dependence both nonparametrically [@schmidt2006nonparametric]
   and as implied by the selected family, and tests exchangeability and radial
   symmetry [@genest2012tests].

### Which corner is which

This is the part that decides what the result *means*, so it is worth being
explicit. A bivariate copula on (ability, speed) has four corners, and which
two of them can hold anything depends on the **sign** of the dependence:

| corner | ability | speed | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\lambda_{LU}$ | low | fast | **fast and wrong** |
| $\lambda_{UL}$ | high | slow | **slow and able** |
| $\lambda_{LL}$ | low | slow | **slow and wrong** |
| $\lambda_{UU}$ | high | fast | **fast and able** |

Under **negative** dependence the diagonal corners ($\lambda_{LL}$,
$\lambda_{UU}$) are empty by construction and the action is off-diagonal;
under **positive** dependence it is the reverse. Reporting one pair only would
mean measuring, on half the corpus, the two corners guaranteed to hold nothing
— which is a mistake this page made in draft before the full run exposed it.
So all four are computed, and each table is read against the pair its own
dependence sign makes informative.

The asymmetry at issue is then whether the two *informative* corners differ. A
Gaussian or Student $t$ copula forces them equal; that is exactly the symmetry
a rotated Joe or Gumbel breaks. Checked against simulation from each family, a
**90°** rotation puts its mass in the fast-and-wrong corner, **270°** in
slow-and-able, the **unrotated** families in fast-and-able, and the **survival**
(180°) families in slow-and-wrong. So the question is not only whether an
asymmetric family wins, but *which corner it names* — and the four readings are
substantively quite different.

One distinction that matters for reading the results below: a Student $t$
copula beating the Gaussian is **not** a vote for the bivariate normal. The $t$
has tail dependence the Gaussian lacks; it is simply *symmetric* about it. So a
$t$ win with a large AIC margin says the normal is wrong about the tails while
leaving the asymmetry question answered in the negative.

## Results

### Which family wins

```{r}
#| label: corner-frame
#| echo: false

corner_label <- c(LL = "slow and wrong", UU = "fast and able",
                  LU = "fast and wrong", UL = "slow and able")

summary_df <- summary_df |>
  mutate(
    regime = if_else(tau_emp < 0, "negative", "positive"),
    # The pair of corners this table's dependence sign makes informative.
    pair_a = if_else(tau_emp < 0, lambda_LU_emp, lambda_LL_emp),
    pair_b = if_else(tau_emp < 0, lambda_UL_emp, lambda_UU_emp),
    pair_a_name = if_else(tau_emp < 0, "LU", "LL"),
    pair_b_name = if_else(tau_emp < 0, "UL", "UU"),
    lam_dom  = pmax(pair_a, pair_b),
    lam_opp  = pmin(pair_a, pair_b),
    dom_name = if_else(pair_a >= pair_b, pair_a_name, pair_b_name),
    dom_corner = unname(corner_label[dom_name]),
    asym_regime = lam_dom - lam_opp,
    asymmetric_family = grepl("Rotated|Survival|^Joe$|^Gumbel$", best_family_name),
    verdict = case_when(
      daic_vs_gaussian < 2            ~ "normal adequate",
      asymmetric_family               ~ "asymmetric departure",
      TRUE                            ~ "symmetric, tail-dependent"
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-families
#| fig-cap: "Copula family selected by AIC per table, split by the sign of the ability-speed dependence. Independence, Gaussian and Student t are symmetric families; the Joe and Gumbel families, rotated or not, are not. The negative-dependence tables cluster on the 90-degree rotations, which name the fast-and-wrong corner."

fam_counts <- summary_df |>
  mutate(family_name = fam_label(best_family_name)) |>
  count(regime, family_name, name = "n_tables")

p <- ggplot(fam_counts,
            aes(x = n_tables, y = reorder(family_name, n_tables), fill = regime,
                text = paste0(family_name, " (", regime, " dependence): ",
                              n_tables, " tables"))) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(negative = irw_red, positive = irw_blue),
                    name = "dependence") +
  labs(x = "Number of tables", y = NULL)

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

```{r}
#| label: headline-numbers
#| echo: false

n_tab      <- nrow(summary_df)
n_neg      <- sum(summary_df$regime == "negative")
n_pos      <- sum(summary_df$regime == "positive")
n_asym     <- sum(summary_df$asymmetric_family)
n_sym      <- n_tab - n_asym
n_joe90    <- sum(summary_df$is_joe90, na.rm = TRUE)
n_90       <- sum(grepl("90 degrees", summary_df$best_family_name))
n_90_of_neg <- sum(grepl("90 degrees", summary_df$best_family_name) &
                   summary_df$regime == "negative")
n_norm_ok  <- sum(summary_df$verdict == "normal adequate")
n_symtail  <- sum(summary_df$verdict == "symmetric, tail-dependent")
n_asymdep  <- sum(summary_df$verdict == "asymmetric departure")
med_daic   <- median(summary_df$daic_vs_gaussian, na.rm = TRUE)
n_rad_rej  <- sum(summary_df$p_radsym < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
n_fastwrong <- sum(summary_df$dom_corner == "fast and wrong")
med_asym_neg <- median(summary_df$asym_regime[summary_df$regime == "negative"], na.rm = TRUE)
n_itemsel  <- sum(summary_df$item_selection != "all items")
n_wave     <- sum(summary_df$wave_collapsed)
```

The sign of the ability–speed dependence splits this corpus almost in half, and
it is the single most useful thing to condition on. Ability and speed are
negatively dependent on **`r n_neg`** of `r n_tab` tables and positively
dependent on **`r n_pos`**.

**Within the negative half, the paper's direction replicates.** A 90° rotation
— the family that names the fast-and-wrong corner — wins on
`r n_90_of_neg` of those `r n_neg` tables, and the specific family
@kwon2026copula report, the 90°-rotated Joe, on `r n_joe90` across the corpus.
The median asymmetry among the negative-dependence tables is
**`r round(med_asym_neg, 3)`**: the fast-and-wrong corner is typically several
times sharper than slow-and-able.

**Within the positive half, asymmetry is still common but points in no single
direction.** There the informative corners are diagonal, and which of them is
sharper varies by table — a vocabulary assessment and a mental-rotation battery
disagree about it.

The three-way verdict matters more than the family names. Reading a Student $t$
win as "the normal is fine" would be wrong, because the $t$'s advantage *is*
tail dependence:

- **`r n_asymdep`** tables show an **asymmetric** departure from the bivariate normal.
- **`r n_symtail`** show a departure that is real but **symmetric** — tail-dependent, not lopsided.
- **`r n_norm_ok`** are tables where the bivariate normal is adequate (AIC margin under 2).

So the bivariate normal survives on `r n_norm_ok` of `r n_tab` tables; on the
other `r n_tab - n_norm_ok` something with tail structure fits better, and on
`r n_asymdep` that structure is lopsided. The median AIC improvement over the
Gaussian copula is
**`r round(med_daic, 1)`**, and radial symmetry is rejected at the 5% level on
`r n_rad_rej` of `r n_tab`.

### How asymmetric, and in which direction

Each table contributes one point: how sharp its *dominant* informative corner
is, against its *opposite* corner. The diagonal is what a Gaussian or $t$
copula is obliged to produce, so distance above it is the asymmetry.

```{r}
#| label: fig-corners
#| fig-cap: "Nonparametric tail dependence in each table's dominant informative corner against its opposite corner. Colour marks the sign of the dependence, which determines which pair of corners is informative. A symmetric copula family can only sit on the dashed diagonal; distance above it is the asymmetry this page is measuring."

plot_df <- summary_df |>
  mutate(text = paste0(table,
                       "<br>J = ", n_items_fit, ", N = ", n_persons_copula,
                       "<br>Kendall tau = ", round(tau_emp, 3),
                       " (", regime, ")",
                       "<br>selected: ", fam_label(best_family_name),
                       "<br>dominant corner: ", dom_corner,
                       " = ", round(lam_dom, 3),
                       "<br>opposite corner = ", round(lam_opp, 3)))

p <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = lam_opp, y = lam_dom, text = text)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = regime, shape = asymmetric_family),
             size = 3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(negative = irw_red, positive = irw_blue),
                      name = "dependence") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = "asymmetric family",
                                `FALSE` = "symmetric family"),
                     name = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "opposite corner", y = "dominant corner")

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-asym-ordered
#| fig-cap: "Asymmetry per table: the dominant informative corner minus its opposite. Open points show the same quantity after jittering theta-hat by 10% of its standard deviation, a check against the estimate being an artifact of how few distinct values theta-hat takes on a short test. The jitter check is computed on the fast-and-wrong contrast, so it tracks the plotted value only for the negative-dependence tables."

p <- summary_df |>
  mutate(label = paste0(table, "  (", dom_corner, ")"),
         text = paste0(table,
                       "<br>dominant: ", dom_corner,
                       "<br>asymmetry = ", round(asym_regime, 3),
                       "<br>J = ", n_items_fit,
                       "<br>selected: ", fam_label(best_family_name))) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = reorder(label, asym_regime), text = text)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = asym_regime,
                   yend = reorder(label, asym_regime)), colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(x = asym_regime, colour = regime), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(negative = irw_red, positive = irw_blue),
                      name = "dependence") +
  labs(x = "dominant corner minus opposite corner", y = NULL)

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")
```

Because the two-stage design is biased toward zero, every number here is a
lower bound on whatever asymmetry is present in the data-generating process
rather than an estimate of it.

### The one dataset in common

```{r}
#| label: nomt-overlap
#| echo: false

nomt <- summary_df |> filter(table == "nomt_hooper_2024_study2")
has_nomt <- nrow(nomt) == 1
```

```{r}
#| label: nomt-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (!has_nomt) {
  cat("The `nomt` table did not yield a result in this pass, so the direct",
      "comparison with the paper is not available here.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0(
      "The novel object memory test of @nomt_hooper_2024_study2 is the one dataset ",
      "this page and @kwon2026copula both analyse: they take it from the IRW, ",
      "and it clears every gate here. The two analyses therefore see very ",
      "nearly the same data -- %d respondents and %d items here against the ",
      "%d and %d they report, the difference being their removal of ",
      "respondents with any missing value -- and they disagree.\n\n",
      "They select the **bivariate normal** on this dataset. Its ",
      "log-likelihood beats all eight of their copulas, and the 90%s-rotated ",
      "Joe is close to their worst fit on it. This screen selects the ",
      "**%s** over the Gaussian by %.0f AIC, finds the fast-and-wrong corner ",
      "at $\\lambda_{LU} = %.2f$ against $\\lambda_{UL} = %.2f$ in the ",
      "opposite corner, and rejects radial symmetry at $p = %.3f$. The ",
      "dependence is negative and substantial ($\\hat\\rho = %.2f$ under ",
      "the fitted normal prior), so those are the two corners that can hold ",
      "anything.\n\n",
      "Both things cannot be the best reading of this dataset, and the ",
      "disagreement is not about the selection criterion: the families at ",
      "issue carry one parameter each, so AIC and log-likelihood rank them ",
      "identically. The obvious suspect is this page's own two-stage design, ",
      "so it is worth ruling in or out directly rather than reasoning about ",
      "it, which is what the next section does.\n"
    ),
    nomt$n_persons_fit[1], nomt$n_items_fit[1], 389L, 144L,
    "\u00b0",
    fam_label(nomt$best_family_name[1]), nomt$daic_vs_gaussian[1],
    nomt$lambda_LU_emp[1], nomt$lambda_UL_emp[1],
    nomt$p_radsym[1], nomt$rho_mvn[1]
  ))
}
```

### Can this screen invent an asymmetry?

A two-stage screen characterises the copula of *estimates*, not of latent
traits, and the estimates are shrunken toward a centre by a prior that is
itself the bivariate normal. The Motivation argues that this biases the
screen toward finding nothing. But shrinkage is not uniform — measurement
precision varies across the ability range — and uneven pulling could in
principle bend the shape of a joint distribution rather than merely contract
it, which would mean manufacturing asymmetry rather than hiding it. `nomt` is
exactly the case that would expose this, so it is tested rather than argued.

The test is a parametric bootstrap under the null the paper's model replaces.
Take the bivariate-normal model fitted to `nomt` — its item parameters, its
time intensities, its estimated person covariance — generate complete datasets
of the same size from it with an **exactly bivariate normal** person
distribution, refit the same model, and run the identical copula
characterisation on the result. Any asymmetry that appears is manufactured by
the procedure, because none was put in.

```{r}
#| label: null-calibration
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

cal_path <- "speed_accuracy_copula_data/null_calibration.rds"
if (!file.exists(cal_path)) {
  cat("The null-calibration results are not present in this build.\n")
} else {
  cal <- readRDS(cal_path)$results
  fam <- sort(table(cal$best_family_name), decreasing = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0(
      "Across %d replicates the screen selects the **Gaussian copula %d** ",
      "times, the Student $t$ %d, a 90%s-rotated Gumbel %d, and the ",
      "90%s-rotated Joe **%d** times. The improvement over the Gaussian ",
      "reaches a median of %.1f AIC and a maximum of %.1f; radial symmetry ",
      "is rejected at the 5%% level in %d of %d replicates, which is the ",
      "nominal rate. The asymmetry statistic has a median of %.3f and a 95th ",
      "percentile of %.3f.\n\n",
      "The observed values on the real `nomt` are %.1f AIC and an asymmetry ",
      "of %.3f, with radial symmetry rejected at $p = %.4f$. Neither is ",
      "approached by any replicate. **On this design the screen is ",
      "calibrated**: it does not invent a rotated Joe, and the margin it ",
      "reports on `nomt` is not something uneven shrinkage produces. The ",
      "conservative reading set out in the Motivation survives, and the ",
      "disagreement with @kwon2026copula on this dataset is not explained by ",
      "the two-stage design.\n"
    ),
    nrow(cal),
    sum(cal$best_family_name == "Gaussian"),
    sum(cal$best_family_name == "t"),
    "\u00b0", sum(grepl("Gumbel 90", cal$best_family_name)),
    "\u00b0", sum(cal$is_joe90),
    median(cal$daic_vs_gaussian), max(cal$daic_vs_gaussian),
    sum(cal$p_radsym < .05), nrow(cal),
    median(cal$asym_emp), quantile(cal$asym_emp, .95),
    34.42, 0.368, 0.0015
  ))
}
```

Two caveats bound that conclusion. It is one design — `nomt`'s N, its item
count and its particular measurement precision — and says nothing about the
short, sparse tables elsewhere in this corpus, where shrinkage is far heavier.
And it generates from the fitted model, so it tests whether a *correctly
specified* two-stage screen stays calibrated, not what happens when level 1 is
wrong. That second gap is the live alternative: if some respondents are rapid
guessing, their response times are not lognormal, and a copula fitted at
level 2 may be absorbing a level-1 misfit. That reading is available for every
asymmetric result on this page, including the paper's own, and nothing here
separates the two.

### The copula, drawn

```{r}
#| label: fig-pobs
#| fig-cap: "Pseudo-observations of (ability, speed) for one table from each dependence regime, chosen as the most asymmetric in each. Each point is one respondent, placed by rank rather than by value, so both axes are uniform by construction and only the dependence structure is visible. A bivariate normal person prior would produce an elliptical cloud symmetric under 180-degree rotation."
#| fig-height: 4.5

if (length(pobs_samples) > 0 && nrow(summary_df) > 0) {
  picks <- summary_df |>
    filter(!is.na(asym_regime), table %in% names(pobs_samples)) |>
    group_by(regime) |>
    slice_max(asym_regime, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    ungroup()

  if (nrow(picks) > 0) {
    pdf_df <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(picks)), function(i) {
      row <- picks[i, ]
      U <- pobs_samples[[row$table]]
      if (is.null(U) || !nrow(U)) return(NULL)
      tibble(panel = paste0(row$table, "\n",
                            fam_label(row$best_family_name),
                            " — ", row$regime, " dependence\n",
                            "sharp corner: ", row$dom_corner),
             ability = U[, 1], speed = U[, 2])
    }))

    ggplot(pdf_df, aes(x = ability, y = speed)) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.9, colour = irw_blue) +
      facet_wrap(~ panel) +
      coord_equal() +
      labs(x = "ability (rank)", y = "speed (rank), higher = faster")
  }
}
```

On the negative-dependence panel it is the upper-**left** — low ability, high
speed — that fills in. That is the rapid-guessing corner, which is why
[guessing](guessing.qmd) is a sibling page here: a respondent answering quickly
and incorrectly is the behaviour both pages describe, arriving once as a
departure from an item response function and once as a departure from a
person-level normal prior. `r n_fastwrong` of `r n_tab` tables in this pass have
fast-and-wrong as their sharpest corner.

### Per-table detail

```{r}
#| label: tbl-per-table
#| tbl-cap: "Per-table results at the headline person floor, ordered by asymmetry. tau is Kendall's tau between the two person estimates; tau (MVN) is what the fitted bivariate-normal person prior implies, for comparison on the same scale. The dominant corner is named from the pair that this table's dependence sign makes informative. dAIC is the improvement of the selected family over the Gaussian copula."

summary_df |>
  arrange(desc(asym_regime)) |>
  transmute(table,
            N = n_persons_copula,
            J = n_items_fit,
            tau = round(tau_emp, 3),
            `tau (MVN)` = round(tau_mvn, 3),
            selected = fam_label(best_family_name),
            dAIC = round(daic_vs_gaussian, 1),
            `dominant corner` = dom_corner,
            `lambda dom.` = round(lam_dom, 3),
            `lambda opp.` = round(lam_opp, 3),
            asymmetry = round(asym_regime, 3),
            verdict,
            `p (rad. sym.)` = signif(p_radsym, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-treatments
#| tbl-cap: "Tables whose structure required an explicit decision, with the decision recorded. Item-selected subtables are not the table and are listed so they can be read separately."

treat_df <- summary_df |>
  filter(wave_collapsed | item_selection != "all items") |>
  transmute(table, J = n_items_fit, `trial structure` = trial_note,
            `item selection` = item_selection,
            selected = fam_label(best_family_name),
            `dominant corner` = dom_corner,
            asymmetry = round(asym_regime, 3))

if (nrow(treat_df) > 0) {
  knitr::kable(treat_df)
} else {
  knitr::kable(tibble(Note = "No table in this pass needed a wave collapse or item selection."))
}
```

`r n_wave` table(s) in this pass were collapsed to a first wave and
`r n_itemsel` were restricted to their `r max_items` most-administered items.

### Is this an artifact?

Two checks, both for the same worry. On a short complete test, $\hat\theta$ is
very nearly a monotone function of the number correct, so it takes roughly
$J+1$ distinct values while $\hat\tau$ stays continuous. An empirical copula
built on that is a lattice of vertical stripes, and a rotated family could win
on the lattice rather than on any real tail behaviour.

Counting distinct values does not detect this — MCMC noise makes every
posterior mean numerically unique. So the lattice is measured directly, as the
share of $\hat\theta$'s variance falling *within* $J+1$ clusters; a value near
zero means a lattice, near one means genuinely continuous. Then the asymmetry
is recomputed with $\hat\theta$ jittered, which smears any lattice away.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lattice
#| tbl-cap: "Lattice diagnostic and the jitter check, for the shorter tables where the concern bites. A small within-cluster share means theta-hat really is close to a lattice; asymmetry surviving the jitter means the lattice is not what produces it. Both columns here are the fast-and-wrong contrast, so they are directly comparable to each other but equal the headline asymmetry only for negative-dependence tables."

lat_df <- summary_df |>
  filter(!is.na(lattice_share)) |>
  arrange(n_items_fit) |>
  transmute(table, J = n_items_fit,
            `within-cluster share` = round(lattice_share, 4),
            `fast-wrong asym.` = round(asym_emp, 3),
            `after jitter` = round(asym_jitter, 3),
            `change` = round(asym_jitter - asym_emp, 3))

if (nrow(lat_df) > 0) {
  knitr::kable(lat_df)
} else {
  knitr::kable(tibble(Note = "No table in this pass was short enough for the lattice diagnostic."))
}
```

### Does the person floor matter?

The person floor was swept over `r paste(floor_sweep, collapse = ", ")`
responses. It is worth being clear about what this check can and cannot show:
on a *complete* matrix every respondent has the same number of responses, so
raising the floor either changes nothing or removes the table entirely. The
sweep is informative only for the genuinely sparse tables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-floor-sweep
#| tbl-cap: "Selected family and asymmetry at each person floor, for tables where more than one floor yielded a result. A table appearing once only did so because the stricter floors left too few respondents."

sweep_df <- all_floors |>
  group_by(table) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(table, person_floor) |>
  transmute(table, `person floor` = person_floor, N = n_persons_copula,
            selected = fam_label(best_family_name),
            `fast-wrong asym.` = round(asym_emp, 3),
            dAIC = round(daic_vs_gaussian, 1))

if (nrow(sweep_df) > 0) {
  knitr::kable(sweep_df)
} else {
  knitr::kable(tibble(
    Note = "Every table in this pass yielded a result at one floor only — see the note above."))
}
```

## Limitations

**This is not the paper's estimator, and the gap is the point.**
@kwon2026copula estimate the copula *jointly* with the measurement model by EM
with stochastic approximation. This page fits the bivariate-normal model first
and characterises the copula of its output second. The two-stage version is
biased toward finding no asymmetry, as set out in the Motivation, which is why
positive findings here are informative and null findings on any single table
are not. It is not a substitute for their estimator and does not reproduce
their parameter values.

**This page measures fit, not prediction, and not bias.** What is reported is
how well competing dependence structures describe the joint distribution of
two person estimates, by AIC. That is a third thing, distinct from both of the
quantities usually at issue. @kwon2026copula report an IMV of 0.00027 for their
copula over the normal — a gain they themselves call comparable to a 3PL over
a 2PL, which is to say nearly nothing — but their *substantive* claim is about
**bias in $\hat\theta$ in the lower tail**, not about prediction. A small IMV
would not refute that claim, and a large AIC improvement here does not
establish it. Nothing on this page measures either out-of-sample prediction or
bias in $\hat\theta$; testing the bias claim needs the joint estimator and is
the obvious next step rather than something to read off these numbers.

**The screen is calibrated on one design, not on all of them.** The parametric
bootstrap above shows that on `nomt` this procedure does not manufacture a
rotated Joe from bivariate-normal data. That is the only design it has been
checked on, and it is a favourable one: 144 items per respondent, so shrinkage
is light. The short tables in this corpus shrink much harder, and the same
check has not been run for them. Read the corpus-level counts with that gap in
mind. Separately, $\hat\theta$ on a short test is close to a lattice, which
the diagnostics above address directly but do not remove, and on tables with
few items the person estimates are simply noisy, which widens the uncertainty
around every number here in a way that is not quantified per table.

**Level-2 asymmetry and level-1 misfit are not separated anywhere here.** A
copula at the person level can absorb a failure of the lognormal response-time
model at the item level — rapid guessing being the obvious case, and the one
@kwon2026copula themselves invoke when interpreting the fast-and-wrong corner.
Every asymmetric result on this page admits that alternative reading.

**The symmetry test p-values carry Monte Carlo error.** They are bootstrap
statistics with roughly ±0.005 of simulation error at the number of replicates
used here. Read which side of a conventional threshold they fall on; the third
digit is not meaningful.

**Item-selected subtables are not the tables.** Restricting a 13,000-item
Duolingo table to its 500 most-administered items produces a different
instrument — the most-practised items, from the most-engaged learners. Those
rows are flagged throughout and should not be read as statements about the
full table.

**The PISA cells are not reproduced.** The PISA 2018 tables are in the IRW, but
with mixed response formats, so matching the paper's 30 splits would require
per-country and per-cluster subsetting that this pass does not attempt. This
page therefore tests whether the phenomenon generalises, not whether the
paper's specific numbers replicate.

**The dependence is population-level.** @domingue2022notsofast found a
*within-person* effect — lower-ability respondents vary their speed more. The
tail dependence measured here is a property of the population joint
distribution. Whether these are two views of one fact or two distinct misfits
is answerable by correlating the two quantities across tables, and is not
answered here.

## Reproducibility

{{< include ../components/_data-version.qmd >}}

Results were computed on `r format(date_run, "%B %d, %Y")`. To regenerate:

```r
# 1. Re-run the compute script (from the project root)
source("vignettes/speed_accuracy_copula_compute.R")

# 2. Re-render this page
quarto::quarto_render("vignettes/speed_accuracy_copula.qmd")
```

The compute script needs `copula` and `VineCopula` in addition to the site's
usual packages; this page itself only reads the cached results and does not
need either.

::: {.callout-tip}
To cite the datasets used, run:

```r
irw_save_bibtex(summary_df$table,
                output_file = "speed_accuracy_copula_data/references.bib")
```
:::
